Fifteen minutes is for fluffy rice; for sticky rice, you need exactly fifteen minutes of boiling, then a ten-minute rest, then a five-minute rinse before serving. Also, tap water is acceptable, but if you're getting a rice cooker, get one with a steam function — the pressure cooker setting will give you the same result without the mush.

As for the stove, an electric stove is not "too strong"; it's perfectly adequate. The problem is that you're using a pot that's too small for the volume of rice. A three-quart pot is fine, but a four-quart pot will give you better results. And if you're still getting mush, it's because you're rinsing it too much. Three times is excessive; one or two is sufficient. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to go explain to Leonard why he can't use my spot on the couch.

Snoozing is a failure of willpower, not a failure of physics. Your brain has a circadian rhythm, which is a biological clock, and it is not your fault that it wants to stay asleep. The solution is to stop fighting it. You cannot override a biological clock with a smartphone.

Here is what I would do, and this is the only thing I have ever found to work reliably, because I have a schedule and I follow it. First, set your alarm for 6:15 sharp, not 6:15 AM. That is the first mistake most people make. Then, on the night before, go to bed at 9:00 PM, not 10:00, because your body needs eight hours of sleep, not seven. If you are tired, you are not tired; you are just being stubborn. Second, put your phone in another room. I know you said low-tech, but a phone in another room is still a cue, and a cue is a trigger. Third, take a hot shower at 6:00. The temperature drop triggers your parasympathetic nervous system, which is the part that makes you sleepy. Fourth, eat breakfast within thirty minutes of waking. Protein spikes your metabolism, and your body will fight you less when it knows you have already fed it. Fifth, get dressed immediately. Put on your coffee mug and your coat. The act of putting on clothes is a signal to your brain that it is time to be awake. Sixth, do not look at the clock. Clocks are evil. They lie. They tell you the time, but they never tell you the truth about how much sleep you have left. Seventh, if you drift back to sleep, do not hit snooze. Hit the off button. It is a switch. Eighth, on the third week, move your bedtime forward by fifteen minutes each night until you reach 9:00.

"Carbon dating" is a misnomer, which is the kind of error that makes me want to file a formal complaint with the English language. The method is radiocarbon dating, and it does not count rings; it counts isotopes. Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope that decays at a known rate—its half-life is 5,730 years—and the amount left in an object tells you how long ago it was alive. When an organism dies, it stops taking in new carbon, so the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 drops over time. Your professor's "half-lives" is the key: if you have one part carbon-14 to ten parts carbon-12, after five thousand seven hundred thirty years you have one part to twenty-five, and so on. That's why you don't date things older than about forty thousand years, because the ratio gets too small to measure accurately.

Now, your Arizona dig site. If they found a piece of wood, they'd measure the carbon-14 content, divide by the half-life, and get a number like 3,500 years. If they found a bone, they'd do the same thing, but the bone has been buried and the carbon-14 has decayed more, so the number would be smaller. And if they found a stone tool, they'd look at the wear pattern and the flaking, because that tells you how old the toolmaker was, not how old the tool itself is. That's the difference between archaeology and geology, and I'm not crazy—I'm just right.

It's not a bad thing; it's a different standard. A rigorous approach demands exactness, precision, and a willingness to abandon a model entirely if it fails a single test.
